title: JVM, JDK and JRE
context: What is the difference between the JVM, the JDK and the JRE?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java basics questions (1 of 3)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) runs compiled bytecode. It loads classes, verifies them, and executes them, and it provides garbage collection and a platform-independent runtime. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the standard class libraries, enough to run Java programs. The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus development tools such as the compiler `javac`, `jar` and `javadoc`. To build and run code, install the JDK. To only run an app, the JRE is enough.

points.title: JVM runs bytecode
points.why: The JVM is the runtime that executes .class files. This is what makes Java portable across operating systems.

points.title: JRE is JVM plus libraries
points.why: The JRE adds the standard library to the JVM so programs can run. It has no compiler.

points.title: JDK adds development tools
points.why: The JDK contains javac and other tools needed to write and build code.
